reference_material: A matrix is in reduced row-echelon form if the leading entry of each nonzero row is a 1 (a leading 1), each leading 1 is the only nonzero entry in its column, and each leading 1 sits to the right of every leading 1 in the rows above it. The row-reduced form of a system's augmented matrix lets us determine the solution set directly, since each leading-1 column corresponds to a variable whose value is read off immediately from the row, without needing to substitute values back through the other equations.

reference_material: Given a set of vectors S, their span is the set of all possible linear combinations of the vectors in S. The span provides a compact way to describe an infinite set of vectors: rather than listing every vector in the set, we describe it as everything reachable by scaling and adding together the vectors in S.

reference_material: A set of vectors is linearly independent when the only way to write the zero vector as a linear combination of them is the trivial way, using all-zero coefficients. If some other, nontrivial combination of the vectors also produces the zero vector, the set is linearly dependent, and at least one vector in the set is redundant -- it can be written as a linear combination of the others.

reference_material: A subset S of a vector space V is a basis of V if it is linearly independent and spans V. The spanning requirement ensures S has enough raw material to build every vector in V, while the linear independence requirement ensures S contains no more raw material than is needed -- a basis is a minimal spanning set.

reference_material: A linear transformation T from vector space U (the domain) to vector space V (the codomain) is a function with two defining properties: T(u1 + u2) = T(u1) + T(u2) for all u1, u2 in U, and T(alpha*u) = alpha*T(u) for all u in U and every scalar alpha. reference_material: The determinant of a square matrix is a single scalar computed from its entries. A square matrix is nonsingular -- meaning it is invertible and the associated homogeneous system has only the trivial solution -- exactly when its determinant is nonzero; a zero determinant signals that the matrix has no inverse.

reference_material: Cramer's Rule solves a system of linear equations by replacing the coefficient matrix's variable column of interest with the constant column and comparing determinants: each variable's value is the ratio of that modified matrix's determinant to the determinant of the original coefficient matrix. Cramer's Rule gives the unique solution to a system when the coefficient matrix's determinant is nonzero; if that determinant is zero, the system has no solution or infinitely many, and Cramer's Rule cannot be used.

reference_material: Suppose A is a square matrix, x is a nonzero vector, and lambda is a scalar. Then x is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue lambda if A*x = lambda*x. The eigenvalues of A are exactly the roots of A's characteristic polynomial, and for each eigenvalue, the set of eigenvectors together with the zero vector forms a subspace called the eigenspace.

reference_material: Two square matrices A and B of the same size are similar if there exists a nonsingular matrix S such that A = S*B*S^-1. Similar matrices share many important properties, including their eigenvalues; a matrix that is similar to a diagonal matrix is called diagonalizable, and its diagonal entries are exactly its eigenvalues.

reference_material: A square matrix A is stochastic if all of its entries are nonnegative and the entries of each column sum to 1. A difference equation v_(t+1) = A*v_t, where A is a stochastic matrix, is called a Markov chain: it models how a population or probability distribution moves between states from one time step to the next, with each column of A giving the probabilities of moving from that column's state to each other state.

reference_material: Google's PageRank algorithm ranks web pages using the Importance Rule: if a page P links to n other pages, each of those pages inherits 1/n of P's importance. The importance matrix built from this rule is a stochastic matrix, and a page's PageRank is its entry in that matrix's steady-state vector -- the eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 that the Markov chain converges to.
